headline.funnel_interpretation: Egger’s test is generally not recommended when fewer than 10 studies are available.
headline.results_interpretation: The pooled analysis of 2 studies yielded an effect size of 0.95 (95% CI: 0.44–2.04), indicating no statistically significant association between monounsaturated fat (mufa) and bladder cancer. Although the point estimate suggests a potential inverse relationship, the confidence interval includes the null. These findings were accompanied by very high heterogeneity (I² = 88.67%), reflecting highly inconsistent results across studies.

studies.Population: Participants of the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian (PLCO) Cancer Screening Trial
studies.Ethnicity Basis: NA: no field-specific ethnicity evidence was available
studies.Reference: Dietary Fatty Acids and Bladder Cancer Risk: Insights from the PLCO Cancer Screening Trial.
studies.Authors: Li G, Zheng W, Zhang X, Chen Y
studies.comparison_type: Higher vs lower dietary MUFA intake (highest vs lowest category), women
studies.exposure_measurement_supporting_text: the relationship between the consumption of different dietary fatty acids and the risk of bladder cancer

sample_size.excerpt: A quantitative analysis was conducted using data from the Prostate, Lung, Colorectal, and Ovarian (PLCO) Cancer Screening Trial, which included 101,731 participants.

cases.excerpt: During a median follow-up of 11.3 years, 861 bladder cancer cases were identified.

effect_size.excerpt: Gender-specific analysis showed that a higher intake of monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) was linked to a reduced risk of bladder cancer in females (HR: 0.62; 95% CI: 0.39-0.99, P-trend = 0.028). However, restricted cubic spline analysis revealed no linear relationship between MUFA intake and bladder cancer risk in the overall group or gender-specific subgroups.

confidence_interval.excerpt: Gender-specific analysis showed that a higher intake of monounsaturated fatty acids (MUFAs) was linked to a reduced risk of bladder cancer in females (HR: 0.62; 95% CI: 0.39-0.99, P-trend = 0.028).

design.excerpt: The Cox proportional hazards model was used to calculate hazard ratios (HR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for bladder cancer risk
